The Spotfin croaker (Roncador stearnsii) is a common sciaenid inhabiting coastal waters of southern California and Baja California, where it is frequently targeted by recreational anglers. Examination of size-at-maturity data from a long-term field survey of this species revealed that individuals attain puberty at a total length of 17.9 centimeters [Lp = 17.9 centimeters], a relatively modest size that allows for early reproductive engagement. In contrast, the ultimate total length recorded for the species is 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], indicating considerable post-maturity growth capacity. This substantial gape between length at puberty and asymptotic size is typical among iteroparous sciaenids and suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early breeding without severely compromising future fecundity. Field collections spanning several decades indicate that the largest individuals, often females, approach the 70 centimeter mark, although such specimens are increasingly uncommon in heavily fished areas.

At a stable water temperature of 17.8 °C [T = 17.8 °C], reflective of typical late-spring conditions in the Southern California Bight, the embryonic development of Spotfin croaker proceeds rapidly. Field observations of recently spawned eggs collected from nearshore plankton tows indicate that the age at birth, defined as the interval from fertilization to eclosion, is approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days] at this at a temperature of 17.8 °C [T = 17.8 °C]thermal regime. The resulting yolk-sac larva emerges at a remarkably small size; the wet weight at birth is roughly 0.0002 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0002 grams], a mass consistent with the small, pelagic eggs characteristic of the family Sciaenidae. This minuscule initial mass imposes substantial challenges during the early larval phase, as the endotrophic larva must complete yolk absorption and initiate exogenous feeding within a very narrow temporal window.

The daily reproductive rate of the Spotfin croaker has been estimated using fecundity data from gravid females collected during the peak spawning season. At 17.8 °C [T = 17.8 °C], each mature female produces approximately 2,028 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,028 eggs per day] during the spawning period. This figure, derived from the product of batch fecundity and spawning frequency observed in related sciaenids, indicates a substantial daily reproductive output. The combination of a moderate batch size and a protracted spawning season allows this species to achieve high annual fecundity despite individual eggs being very small. The corresponding ultimate wet weight of an adult female is estimated at 4,100 grams [Wwi = 4,100 grams], a body mass that supports the energetic demands of repeated batch spawning through the spring and summer months.

Longevity records for the Spotfin croaker, established through otolith-based age validation studies, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of the Southern California Bight, which average around 17.8 °C [T = 17.8 °C]. This lifespan is comparable to that of other medium-bodied sciaenids in the region, such as the white croaker, and reflects a relatively slow pace of senescence. The age structure of populations in less exploited areas reveals that individuals beyond 10 years of age are regularly encountered, with a small proportion of females persisting into the 15th year. Such extended longevity, combined with iteroparous batch spawning, provides demographic resilience against interannual variability in recruitment success.

While females first become reproductively active at a total length of 17.9 centimeters [Lp = 17.9 centimeters], their body mass continues to increase dramatically, with the ultimate wet weight reaching 4,100 grams [Wwi = 4,100 grams]. The small initial mass of the offspring, 0.0002 grams [Wwb = 0.0002 grams], represents a drastic size discrepancy between the maternal parent and her progeny, a common feature in marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small, pelagic eggs. This life-history configuration, underpinned by a maximum lifespan of roughly 15 years [am = roughly 15 years] at 17.8 °C [T = 17.8 °C], allows the Spotfin croaker to sustain its populations through a combination of early maturation, high fecundity, and extended reproductive tenure.
